text: Johnson's praise of Shakespeare rests upon a single principle, and he states it plainly: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). The dramatists who wrote beside Shakespeare drew men, in Johnson's account, as the customs of a particular court or city had shaped them. Their figures were fitted to the fashions of a season; they spoke the cant of a coterie and turned on the follies of a year. When the season passed, the figures passed with it, and a later reader finds in them only the dress of a vanished time. Shakespeare's persons are of another make. They act and speak by those passions and principles which belong to every age and every country, so that a father's grief or a counsellor's vanity is the same in Elsinore as in London, and the same now as when the plays were first acted. Johnson does not deny that the plays carry the marks of their own day. He holds only that these marks lie on the surface, and that beneath them stands the common nature of mankind. This is why a reader who knows nothing of Elizabethan manners can still believe in Polonius.
